Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

love verb and noun

also be fond of, fondness, loving, be mad about, be madly in love with, be crazy about, affection, affectionate, be infatuated with, passionately, madly in love, fall in love, esteem, he’s crazy about her, fall in love at first sight, love at first sight, be nuts about someone, warm-hearted

classical

Cic. Q. fr. 3.1.7: nōn enim concēdō tibi plūs ut illum amēs quam ipse amō
Ter. Ph. 478: omnēs vōs amō
Traupman 153

amō, amāre, amāvī, amātum

verb, first conjugation

Of people and of things (rūs amat, Ov. Met. 14.627). In comedy and Cicero’s letters amō tē also thanks (Meritō tē amō, Ter. Ad. 945–946), and amābō is “please” (see please).

Other words

  • amor, amōris m. — love

    noun, third declension · classical · Cic. Off. 1.12: praecipuum quendam amōrem in eōs quī prōcreātī sunt; Traupman 153, 149; Traupman 269; Traupman 317

    Also of the one loved: dēliciīs atque amōribus meīs (Cic. Att. 16.6.4).

  • dīligō, dīligere, dīlēxī, dīlēctum — love, hold dear

    verb, third conjugation · also used · classical · Catull. 72.4: sed pater ut gnātōs dīligit et generōs; Cic. Fam. 16.2.1: quantum mē dīligis; Traupman 98: to be fond of, dīligō; Traupman 98: dīligere, be fond of; Traupman 152; Traupman 317

    Lewis & Short: “to value or esteem highly, to love”: the love of regard and choice, as of a father for his children in Catullus.

  • amāns, amantis — loving, fond

    adjective (participle of amō), declension · also used · classical · Lewis & Short, s.v. amō; Andresian p. 36; Traupman 155, 342, 149, 404

    Loving and affectionate, often with the genitive and in the superlative: amantissimus tuī, most devoted to you.

  • dēpereō, dēperīre, dēperiī — be madly in love with, be dying of love for

    verb, irregular, like pereō; with the accusative of the person loved, often with amōre, conjugation · also used · classical · Plaut. Epid. 2.2.35: illa, quam tuus gnātus annōs multōs deamat, dēperit (Lewis & Short s.v. deamō); Plaut. Cist. 1.3.43: is amōre prōjectīciam illam dēperit (Lewis & Short s.v. amor); Traupman 103: to be mad about, dēpereō (+ acc.); Traupman 298

    (vōx cōmica: Plaut.; nōn apud Cic., Verg., Hor., Ov.)

    Literally “to perish (for someone)”. The person is in the accusative, as the object of the passion: illam dēperit, he is crazy about her. Lewis & Short: frequent in Plautus, not in Cicero, Virgil, Horace or Ovid.

  • efflictim amāre — to love desperately, be infatuated with

    also used · classical · Plaut. Am. 1.3.19: ut hic tē efflictim dēperit (Lewis & Short); Traupman 154, 156

    (vōx cōmica: Plaut.)

    Efflictim, “to death, desperately”, goes with amāre and dēperīre.

Examples

  • nōn enim concēdō tibi plūs ut illum amēs quam ipse amō

    For I won’t grant that you love him more than I do.Cic. Q. fr. 3.1.7

  • Mī Geta, omnēs vōs amō.

    My dear Geta, I love you all.Ter. Ph. 478

  • dīlēxī tum tē nōn tantum ut vulgus amīcam, sed pater ut gnātōs dīligit et generōs

    I loved you then not just as the crowd loves a girlfriend, but as a father loves his sons and sons-in-law.Catull. 72.3–4

  • nōn amō tē, Sabidī, nec possum dīcere quārē: hoc tantum possum dīcere, nōn amō tē

    I don’t love you, Sabidius, and I can’t say why; all I can say is this: I don’t love you.Mart. 1.32.1–2

  • Perditē amāre coepit.

    He fell desperately in love.Traupman 152

  • Eam dēperit.

    He’s crazy about her.Traupman 298

  • ūnō aspectū in amōrem incidere

    to fall in love at first sightTraupman 342

  • (amōre) dēperīre aliquem

    to be nuts about someoneTraupman 352

  • aliquem efflīctim amāre

    to be infatuated with someone, love someone desperatelyLewis & Short s.v. efflīgō: efflīctim amāre (Plaut. Am. 1.3.19); Traupman 332

See also I love you, hate, kiss, hug, darling, please.
